questions.q: A 32-year-old man from rural India presents with multiple erythematous nodular lesions over the face and extremities with loss of eyebrows. On examination, there is bilateral thickening of the greater auricular nerves and ulnar nerves. Slit skin smear reveals a bacterial index of 4+. Which type of lepra reaction is most likely if he develops sudden appearance of painful, red, tender nodules over the body?
questions.exp: Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL) / Type 2 lepra reaction occurs in lepromatous (LL) and borderline lepromatous (BL) leprosy. It is an immune complex-mediated (Type III hypersensitivity) reaction presenting as painful, tender, erythematous nodules. High bacterial index (4+) confirms LL leprosy. Treatment is thalidomide or corticosteroids.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with flaccid blisters involving the oral mucosa and skin. Nikolsky's sign is positive. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows intercellular IgG deposits in a 'chicken-wire' pattern. The target antigen most likely involved is:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris (PV) is characterized by flaccid blisters, mucosal involvement, positive Nikolsky's sign, and intercellular IgG deposition on DIF. The target antigen is Desmoglein 3 (DSG3), a desmosomal cadherin. DSG1 is the target in pemphigus foliaceus. BP180/BP230 are targets in bullous pemphigoid. Laminin 332 is the target in mucous membrane pemphigoid.

questions.q: A 70-year-old male presents with tense blisters predominantly on the lower abdomen, thighs, and flexural areas. The blisters heal without scarring. Nikolsky's sign is negative. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) presents in elderly with tense (subepidermal) blisters on flexural areas, negative Nikolsky's sign, and heals without scarring. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at DEJ (targeting BP180 and BP230). It differs from PV (flaccid blisters, positive Nikolsky's). Linear IgA shows linear IgA on DIF. DH shows granular IgA in dermal papillae.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with butterfly-shaped erythema on the malar region, photosensitivity, and oral ulcers. ANA is positive (1:320, homogeneous pattern). Which of the following cutaneous findings is considered specific for systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.exp: Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) is one of the ACR criteria for SLE and is considered a specific cutaneous manifestation. DLE presents as scarring plaques with follicular plugging. Livedo reticularis and Raynaud's phenomenon occur in SLE but are non-specific. Periungual telangiectasia is more characteristic of dermatomyositis and systemic sclerosis.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male farmer presents with an asymmetric pigmented lesion on the back, 1.2 cm in diameter with irregular borders and variegated color (black, brown, and red areas). Dermoscopy shows regression structures and atypical pigment network. The most important prognostic factor for this condition is:
questions.exp: Breslow's tumor thickness (measured in mm from granular layer to deepest point of invasion) is the single most important prognostic factor for melanoma and is the basis of AJCC T staging. Clark's level (anatomical depth of invasion) is less accurate. While ulceration and mitotic rate are important in staging, Breslow thickness remains the primary determinant of prognosis and surgical margins.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with intensely pruritic vesicles on the extensor surfaces of elbows, knees, and buttocks arranged in groups. He also has chronic diarrhea and bloating. IgA antibodies against tissue transglutaminase are elevated. The treatment of choice is:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is associated with celiac disease. Granular IgA deposits in dermal papillae on DIF is pathognomonic. Treatment is dapsone (for rapid symptom relief) combined with a strict gluten-free diet (for long-term control and prevention of intestinal lymphoma). Dapsone alone does not address the underlying gluten sensitivity.

questions.q: A 24-year-old male presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis for 2 weeks. The ulcer has a clean base, indurated margins, and is non-tender. Inguinal lymph nodes are enlarged, non-tender, and rubbery. VDRL is positive at 1:8. The most appropriate treatment is:
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
questions.exp: The presentation is classic primary syphilis (painless indurated ulcer = chancre, non-tender lymphadenopathy). Treatment of choice for primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis is Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million IU IM single dose. Doxycycline is used in penicillin-allergic patients. Azithromycin is no longer recommended due to resistance. Ceftriaxone is used for gonorrhea.

questions.q: A 10-year-old girl presents with areas of hair loss on the scalp with broken hair stubs, scaling, and cervical lymphadenopathy. KOH mount shows spores inside the hair shaft. The most appropriate treatment is:
questions.exp: Tinea capitis (endothrix pattern — spores inside hair shaft, suggesting Trichophyton species) requires systemic antifungal therapy as topicals do not penetrate the hair shaft. Oral griseofulvin (10-20 mg/kg/day for 6-8 weeks) remains the gold standard for tinea capitis in children. Terbinafine is also effective and preferred for Trichophyton species.

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy presents with severe nocturnal pruritus. Examination reveals linear burrows in the finger web spaces, wrists, and genitalia. Several family members are similarly affected. The drug of choice for treatment is:
questions.exp: Permethrin 5% cream is the first-line treatment for scabies and is safe for use in children above 2 months. Applied overnight to the whole body from neck downwards and washed off after 8-14 hours. Lindane is neurotoxic and contraindicated in children. Benzyl benzoate is irritant. Oral ivermectin is used for crusted scabies or when topical therapy fails.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male with chronic plaque psoriasis is being considered for methotrexate therapy. Which baseline investigation is most critical before initiating treatment?
opts: Liver function tests, CBC, and renal function tests
questions.exp: Before initiating methotrexate, baseline investigations must include liver function tests (LFT), complete blood count (CBC), renal function tests (RFT), and chest X-ray. Methotrexate is hepatotoxic and myelosuppressive and is renally excreted. Baseline liver biopsy is no longer routinely recommended; non-invasive markers (FibroScan, serum procollagen III) are preferred.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with recurrent episodes of eczema involving the cheeks, antecubital fossae, and popliteal fossae. There is a family history of asthma and allergic rhinitis. Serum IgE is markedly elevated. Which of the following cytokines plays the central role in the pathogenesis of this condition?
questions.exp: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is driven by Th2 cytokines, primarily IL-4 and IL-13, which promote IgE class switching (IL-4) and impaired skin barrier function (both IL-4 and IL-13 suppress filaggrin expression). Dupilumab (anti-IL-4Ralpha) blocks both IL-4 and IL-13 signaling and is FDA-approved for moderate-to-severe AD. IL-17/IL-23 are key in psoriasis.

questions.q: A 18-year-old female presents with comedones, papules, pustules, and nodular cysts on the face, chest, and back, causing significant scarring. She has tried topical retinoids and oral antibiotics for 6 months without adequate response. The most appropriate next step is:
opts: Increase dose of topical benzoyl peroxide
questions.exp: Oral isotretinoin is the treatment of choice for severe nodulocystic acne or acne resistant to conventional therapy. It is the only drug that targets all four pathogenic factors of acne: sebum production, abnormal follicular keratinization, Cutibacterium acnes colonization, and inflammation. The typical dose is 0.5-1 mg/kg/day for 16-24 weeks. Pregnancy must be excluded due to teratogenicity.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with a well-demarcated erythematous patch with hyperpigmentation on the glans penis recurring at the same site each time he takes a drug for headache. The most common causative drug is:
questions.exp: Fixed drug eruption (FDE) characteristically recurs at the same site upon re-exposure to the offending drug. Cotrimoxazole (TMP-SMX) is the most common cause of FDE worldwide, especially on the genitalia and lips. Lesions heal with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

questions.q: A 25-year-old HIV-positive male presents with painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in a dermatomal distribution over the right thorax restricted to a single dermatome. The most appropriate antiviral treatment is:
questions.exp: Herpes zoster treatment in immunocompromised patients (like HIV) requires higher doses and longer duration. The correct dose is Acyclovir 800mg 5 times daily for 7-10 days. The lower dose (200mg 5x/day) is for herpes simplex. Valacyclovir 1g three times daily and famciclovir 500mg three times daily are alternatives for zoster in immunocompetent patients.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman with Sjogren's syndrome presents with palpable purpura on the lower limbs. Skin biopsy shows neutrophilic infiltration around dermal blood vessels with nuclear dust and extravasated red blood cells. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV) is the most common form of cutaneous vasculitis. Histopathology shows neutrophilic infiltrate around small dermal vessels, karyorrhexis (nuclear dust), fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls, and RBC extravasation. It presents as palpable purpura on dependent areas. LCV is associated with Sjogren's syndrome, infections, drugs, and other systemic diseases.

questions.q: A 30-year-old female presents with depigmented macules on the dorsum of hands and perioral area since 2 years. Wood's lamp examination shows chalk-white fluorescence of the patches. She is otherwise healthy. The first-line treatment for localized vitiligo (less than 10% BSA) on the trunk is:
questions.exp: For localized vitiligo affecting less than 10% BSA on non-sensitive areas, potent topical corticosteroids (class III-IV) are the first-line treatment, applied once daily for 3 months. Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) are preferred for face/genitalia to avoid steroid atrophy. Systemic PUVA and phototherapy are for extensive disease. Surgical options are for stable, refractory disease.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with dry, scaly skin since infancy. The scales are large, brown, adherent, and predominantly affect the extensor surfaces with flexural sparing. Diagnosed with ichthyosis vulgaris. The causative mutation affects:
questions.exp: Ichthyosis vulgaris is the most common inherited ichthyosis (autosomal semi-dominant). It is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the filaggrin (FLG) gene. FLG mutations also predispose to atopic dermatitis and allergic disease. TGM1 mutations cause autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis. ABCA12 mutations cause Harlequin ichthyosis.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with flat-topped, violaceous, polygonal papules on the flexor aspect of the wrists and forearms. The surface shows white lacy lines (Wickham's striae). There are similar lesions in the oral cavity. This condition demonstrates which type of Koebner phenomenon?
questions.exp: Lichen planus (LP) demonstrates the true Koebner phenomenon (Type I), where new lesions appear in sites of trauma in a patient with active disease. True Koebner phenomenon also occurs in psoriasis, vitiligo, and plane warts. The 5 Ps of LP: Pruritic, Purple (violaceous), Polygonal, Planar (flat-topped), and Papular. Wickham's striae are pathognomonic. Oral LP may undergo malignant transformation.

questions.q: A 20-year-old presents with a well-defined patch of non-scarring hair loss over the parietal scalp, with exclamation mark hairs at the periphery. The scalp skin appears normal. Dermoscopy reveals yellow dots and black dots. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Alopecia areata (AA) is an autoimmune non-scarring hair loss. Pathognomonic features include: exclamation mark hairs (tapered hair shafts), yellow dots (dilated infundibula with sebum), and black dots (broken hairs at scalp level) on dermoscopy. The scalp is normal without scaling (differentiating from tinea). Trichotillomania shows broken hairs in varied patterns with coiled hairs on dermoscopy.

questions.q: A 42-year-old fair-skinned woman presents with persistent central facial redness, telangiectasias, and repeated episodes of flushing triggered by hot beverages, spicy food, and alcohol. She has papules and pustules but no comedones. The underlying pathophysiology involves:
opts: Neurovascular dysregulation and Demodex folliculorum overgrowth
Type IV hypersensitivity to bacterial antigens
questions.exp: Rosacea is characterized by chronic neurovascular dysregulation (flushing, persistent erythema, telangiectasias) and inflammation. Demodex folliculorum mite overgrowth stimulates innate immune responses via TLR2, releasing cathelicidins. There are no comedones (unlike acne). Treatment includes topical metronidazole, azelaic acid, ivermectin, and oral doxycycline for inflammatory lesions.

questions.q: A 52-year-old woman presents with photosensitivity, blistering on sun-exposed areas (dorsum of hands), hypertrichosis on the temples, and hyperpigmentation. Urine shows pink fluorescence under Wood's lamp. Liver biopsy shows iron overload. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is the most common porphyria. It presents with photoblistering on sun-exposed areas, hypertrichosis (temples, cheeks), hyperpigmentation, and sclerodermoid changes. Urine shows pink-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp (elevated uroporphyrin). It is associated with hepatic iron overload, HCV, HIV, alcohol, and estrogens. Treatment is phlebotomy and low-dose hydroxychloroquine.

questions.q: A 65-year-old male with a long history of chronic plaque psoriasis presents with a solitary, erythematous, scaly plaque that has become indurated and irregular over 8 months. Biopsy shows neoplastic T-lymphocyte infiltration in the epidermis forming Pautrier microabscesses. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Mycosis fungoides (MF) is the most common primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Pautrier microabscesses (clusters of atypical T-lymphocytes within the epidermis) are pathognomonic. MF typically progresses through patch, plaque, and tumor stages. Sezary syndrome is the leukemic variant with erythroderma, Sezary cells in blood, and lymphadenopathy.

questions.q: A 60-year-old renal transplant recipient on long-term cyclosporine presents with multiple keratotic papules on sun-exposed areas with crusted, verrucous appearances. The patient is at highest risk for which malignancy?
questions.exp: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is 65-250 times more common in solid organ transplant recipients on immunosuppression, making it the most common skin cancer in this population (unlike the general population where BCC predominates). HPV infection, UV exposure, and immunosuppression all contribute. These SCCs behave more aggressively with higher rates of metastasis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with recurrent painful oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. She has erythema nodosum on her legs and a positive pathergy test. The most appropriate initial treatment to prevent ocular damage is:
questions.exp: Behcet's disease is a systemic vasculitis characterized by the triad of recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. Ocular involvement is the most serious complication and can lead to blindness. Treatment for severe ocular disease includes azathioprine (to prevent relapses), combined with systemic corticosteroids for acute flares. Biologics (infliximab, adalimumab) are used for refractory cases.

questions.q: A 48-year-old male presents with progressive skin thickening of the fingers (sclerodactyly), Raynaud's phenomenon, and dysphagia. He has perioral skin tightening (microstomia) and calcinosis. ANA shows a nucleolar pattern. The most specific antibody for diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis is:
questions.exp: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is specific for diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) and is associated with interstitial lung disease. Anti-centromere antibody (ACA) is associated with limited cutaneous SSc (CREST syndrome). Anti-Jo-1 is associated with dermatomyositis/antisynthetase syndrome. Anti-Ro is associated with SLE and Sjogren's syndrome.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with widespread erythematous patches and plaques covering more than 90% of his body surface area with diffuse scaling, edema, and warmth. Temperature is 38.5 degrees C and albumin is 2.1 g/dL. The most common cause of erythroderma in adults is:
questions.exp: Erythroderma (exfoliative dermatitis) affecting more than 90% BSA has multiple causes. In adults, the most common cause is psoriasis (25-40%), followed by drug reactions, eczema/atopic dermatitis, and cutaneous lymphoma. Erythroderma is a medical emergency due to thermoregulation failure, protein loss (hypoalbuminemia), high-output cardiac failure, and infection risk.

questions.q: A 16-year-old male presents with a single, dome-shaped, pearly nodule with central umbilication on the forearm. The lesion has been slowly growing for 3 months. Dermoscopy shows a cloverleaf pattern. The causative agent is:
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV), a poxvirus. Characteristic features are pearly, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication containing a cheesy core. Dermoscopy shows a cloverleaf or four-leaf clover pattern with white amorphous lobules. Treatment options include cryotherapy, curettage, imiquimod, or cantharidin.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with proximal muscle weakness, difficulty climbing stairs, and violaceous discoloration of the eyelids (heliotrope rash). She has Gottron's papules over the metacarpophalangeal joints. CK is markedly elevated. The most important investigation to rule out an associated condition is:
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis in adults (especially >45 years) is strongly associated with internal malignancy (15-25% of cases), particularly ovarian, lung, breast, colon, and nasopharyngeal cancers. Heliotrope rash and Gottron's papules are pathognomonic. Malignancy screening with CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis is mandatory at diagnosis and annually for 3-5 years. Anti-TIF1-gamma antibody is most strongly linked to malignancy.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male presents with target lesions on the palms and dorsum of hands following a course of oral co-trimoxazole. He has less than 10% BSA involvement and no mucosal involvement. The most appropriate management is:
opts: Immediate discontinuation of the drug and supportive care
questions.exp: Erythema multiforme minor (EM minor) involves target lesions with less than 10% BSA and no or minimal mucosal involvement, usually triggered by HSV or drugs. Management is primarily supportive after discontinuing the offending drug with antihistamines, topical steroids, and analgesics. Systemic steroids are not routinely recommended for EM minor. IVIG and cyclosporine are reserved for SJS/TEN (>10% BSA with mucosal involvement).

questions.q: During a Tzanck smear from the floor of a fresh blister in a patient with suspected herpes simplex infection, which finding is most characteristic?
opts: Acantholytic cells with peripheral condensation of chromatin
Multinucleated giant cells with steel-grey nuclei (ground-glass appearance)
questions.exp: Tzanck smear in herpes simplex/zoster infections shows multinucleated giant cells with steel-grey or ground-glass nuclear appearance with nuclear molding. This is due to viral cytopathic effect. Acantholytic cells with peripheral chromatin condensation are seen in pemphigus. Eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions (Guarnieri bodies) are seen in poxvirus infections. Tzanck smear cannot differentiate HSV from VZV.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents with scarring alopecia on the vertex scalp. Trichoscopy shows absent follicular openings, peripilar casts, and tuft hairs (polytrichia). Biopsy shows lymphocytic infiltrate at the isthmus level with loss of sebaceous glands. The diagnosis is:
opts: Discoid lupus erythematosus of the scalp
questions.exp: Lichen planopilaris (LPP) is the most common primary lymphocytic scarring alopecia. Hallmark trichoscopy findings include perifollicular erythema and scaling (peripilar casts), absent follicular openings, and tuft hairs. Histology shows lymphocytic infiltrate at the isthmus/infundibulum with sebaceous gland destruction and fibrosis. Frontal fibrosing alopecia is a variant of LPP affecting the hairline.
